questions.questionText: What was the US Civil Rights Movement?

options.text: Struggle against racial segregation in America

questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Movement fought to end segregation and secure voting rights for African Americans.

questions.questionText: Who was Martin Luther King Jr.?

options.text: Baptist minister and leader of non-violent civil rights movement

questions.explanation: MLK led non-violent protests, delivered 'I Have a Dream' speech, was assassinated in 1968.

questions.questionText: What was the Anti-Apartheid Movement?

options.text: Global campaign demanding sanctions against South Africa

questions.explanation: AAM mobilized international pressure through sanctions, boycotts, and awareness campaigns.

questions.questionText: What was the Montgomery Bus Boycott?
questions.explanation: 1955-56 boycott after Rosa Parks' arrest sparked formation of Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

questions.questionText: What was 'people power'?

options.text: Mass civilian mobilization toppling authoritarian regimes

questions.explanation: People power describes mass civilian actions forcing political change, as in Philippines and anti-apartheid protests.

questions.questionText: What was the March on Washington (1963)?
questions.explanation: Historic rally where MLK delivered 'I Have a Dream' speech, demanding jobs and freedom.

questions.questionText: What were sit-ins in the Civil Rights Movement?

options.text: Non-violent protests at segregated lunch counters

questions.explanation: Sit-ins at segregated lunch counters challenged segregation directly, inspiring similar actions nationwide.

questions.questionText: How did civil society protests influence international politics?

options.text: Created global awareness and pressured governments for policy changes

questions.explanation: Movements connected across borders, creating international campaigns and diplomatic pressure.

questions.questionText: What role did women play in civil society protests?

options.text: Led organizations, organized marches, sustained movements

questions.diagram: Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, Albertina Sisulu.
questions.explanation: Women often organized grassroots support, provided resources, and served as movement leaders.

questions.questionText: What was the role of churches in civil rights activism?

options.text: Provided meeting spaces, organizational capacity, and moral framework

questions.diagram: Black churches in America and South Africa.
questions.explanation: Churches served as 'universities of resistance' providing safe spaces and leadership training.

questions.questionText: What was the cultural boycott of South Africa?

options.text: Refusal to perform or attend South African cultural events

questions.explanation: Musicians, actors, and artists refused to perform in South Africa, creating international shame.

questions.questionText: How did student movements contribute to anti-apartheid activism?

options.text: Organized protests, strikes, and connected local to international struggles

questions.explanation: Students organized mass protests, built international networks, and brought global attention to apartheid.

questions.questionText: What was the United Nations' role in anti-apartheid activism?

options.text: Condemned apartheid, passed resolutions, supported liberation movements

questions.explanation: UN passed numerous resolutions condemning apartheid, providing legitimacy to liberation struggle.

questions.questionText: What were freedom rides?

options.text: Interracial groups challenging segregation on interstate transportation

questions.explanation: Freedom Riders deliberately rode interstate buses into segregated South to test Supreme Court rulings.

questions.questionText: Analyze the effectiveness of non-violent protest strategies.

options.text: Gained moral high ground and global sympathy but faced brutal repression

questions.explanation: Non-violence exposed government brutality but required sustained commitment and often combined with other tactics.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the role of solidarity movements in challenging apartheid.

options.text: Provided international legitimacy, resources, and pressure that isolated Pretoria

questions.explanation: Solidarity networks built international campaigns, raised funds for exiles, and pressured their own governments.

questions.questionText: How did civil society protests connect local and global struggles?

options.text: Through shared tactics, international networks, and mutual support

questions.explanation: Activists shared experiences, strategies, and resources across borders, creating transnational movements.

questions.questionText: Analyze the relationship between economic pressure and political change.

options.text: Sanctions and boycotts made apartheid costly and forced negotiations
Economic pressure had no political effect

questions.explanation: Disinvestment campaigns by universities, churches, and governments increased costs of maintaining apartheid.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the legacy of civil society protests for modern activism.

options.text: Established models for global justice movements and human rights campaigns

questions.explanation: Strategies of non-violent resistance, sanctions, and solidarity networks influenced later movements globally.

questions.questionText: How did media coverage influence civil rights movements?

options.text: Television broadcast of protests and repression galvanized global opinion

questions.explanation: TV footage of Birmingham dogs, Freedom Riders, and Sharpeville shocked international opinion and built support.
